facts.fact: Founded 1924 by Paul Murphy; course by H. Chandler Egan, built by Wm. H. Tucker and Sons; clubhouse by Church and Whitehouse; opened August 1925.
Built on the former site of Ladd's Iron Mine Farm; the Ladd Estate Company sold the district with the slogan "Live Where You Play".
The Oregon Iron Company (1865) bought the town, the lake and the ore hills; Oswego was an iron-smelting town until the early 1900s.

The Oswego Iron Furnace (fired 1867) was the first iron furnace on the Pacific Coast: a 32 ft basalt stack shaped like a truncated pyramid with Gothic arches on all four sides. Oregon's oldest industrial landmark, in George Rogers Park.
Finishing holes look over Oswego Lake toward Mt. Hood. Hole 3 is the pond green (the game's course card).

current.subject: A blue anchor with a white keyline (developer's choice, DECISIONS.md 2026-10-18).
current.keep: The anchor, the lake blue and the white: simple, legible, and the only nautical mark in the game.
current.weaknesses: Reads as a generic nautical sticker. The dark outline inside the anchor's counters makes two busy black hooks at 1x, and nothing says which lake.

concepts.name: The Lake Anchor
concepts.rationale: The anchor stays; the white keyline becomes the anchor itself and the blue becomes the lake. A white anchor set on a lake-blue roundel with a single horizon line reads as a club seal rather than a sticker, and the disc gives it one clean silhouette on any card art.
concepts.symbolism: Anchor: lakeside living, the district's "Live Where You Play" pitch. Disc: the lake. The lighter band below the horizon is the water's surface; the anchor sits half above, half below it.
concepts.interpretation: Reading the anchor as the developer's nod to the lake is an interpretation; the anchor has no documented link to the club.
concepts.typography: Cormorant Garamond SemiBold, all caps, wide tracking: a 1920s country-club serif that sits quietly beside a bold mark.
concepts.strengths: Keeps every recognisable element of the original; the disc is the most legible shape at 32 px; one colour family, prints and embroiders as two inks.
concepts.tradeoffs: Roundel-with-anchor is a familiar yacht-club form; it is better executed than the original but not much more ownable.

concepts.name: The Iron Furnace
concepts.rationale: Lake Oswego was an iron town before it was a lake suburb, and the club was laid out on the Ladd Estate's Iron Mine Farm. The 1867 furnace stack is the town's oldest landmark and has a shape no other club owns: a basalt truncated pyramid with a pointed Gothic arch. Drawn with the arch glowing, it is a monument and a hearth at once.
references: Oswego Iron Furnace, George Rogers Park (fact)
Ladd's Iron Mine Farm, the club's site (fact)
concepts.symbolism: Stack: permanence, a century of history before golf. Glowing arch: the hearth of a clubhouse, the warmth of the 19th hole. Two embers: the game's orange accent.
concepts.interpretation: The glow and embers are invented (the furnace has been cold since the 1890s); the stack's shape, stone and arch follow the landmark.
concepts.typography: Bitter SemiBold, all caps: a sturdy slab serif with the feel of cast lettering on a foundry plate.
concepts.strengths: Specific to this town and no other; the silhouette and the lit arch read instantly at 1x; the warm glow stands out from every green card.
concepts.tradeoffs: The furnace is in George Rogers Park, not on the course, so the link runs through the town's and the land's history; it says less about golf or the lake.

recommendation: Concept 2. It is the one mark in the set that could only belong to Lake Oswego, and it is the stronger icon at 32 px. Concept 1 is the safe choice if the lake should stay the story.
